lessons.title: Soil as a living system
lessons.html:
What soil is made of

Soil is a mix of minerals (sand, silt, clay), organic matter, water, air and living organisms. Its physical, chemical and biological properties interact to determine how well crops and pastures grow. Many South African soils are naturally low in organic matter, and some are acidic (much of the eastern high-rainfall areas), sodic or saline (parts of irrigation schemes and drier areas) or shallow. Managing soil means understanding these limits and improving them over time.

Physical properties

  • Texture: the proportion of sand, silt and clay; affects water holding, drainage and workability.
  • Structure: how particles cluster into aggregates; good structure gives pores for air and water.
  • Depth and effective rooting depth: limited by rock, hardpans or wet layers.
  • Bulk density and compaction: heavy machinery on wet soil creates plough pans that restrict roots.

Chemical properties

  • pH: acidic soils reduce availability of phosphorus and can release toxic aluminium.
  • Cation exchange capacity (CEC): the soil's ability to hold nutrients; higher in clay and organic soils.
  • Nutrients: macronutrients (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S) and micronutrients (Zn, B, Mn, Fe, Cu, Mo).
  • Salinity and sodicity.

Biological properties

Bacteria, fungi, earthworms and other organisms decompose residues, cycle nutrients, form aggregates and, in the case of rhizobia, fix nitrogen with legumes. Organic matter feeds this life. Practices that build organic matter, such as residue retention, cover crops and reduced tillage, improve all three property groups together.

lessons.title: Soil sampling, analysis and fertility management
lessons.html:
Measuring before managing

Sampling

  1. Divide the farm into uniform sampling units by soil type, crop history and management.
  2. Take many sub-samples (often 15 to 20) in a zig-zag across each unit with an auger at the correct depth (for example topsoil and, where needed, subsoil).
  3. Avoid unusual spots: old kraals, fertiliser spills, field edges.
  4. Mix sub-samples into one composite sample, label it clearly and send it to an accredited laboratory.
  5. Sample at the same time of year each time so results are comparable.

Interpreting results

The lab report gives pH, nutrient levels, exchangeable cations and often acid saturation. Compare these with crop-specific norms from the laboratory, the Fertilizer Society or an agronomist. Fertiliser and lime recommendations depend on the crop, yield target, soil and economics.

Liming acid soils

Agricultural lime (calcitic or dolomitic) neutralises acidity. It works slowly, must be incorporated or applied well before planting and the rate should be based on analysis. Dolomitic lime also supplies magnesium.

Fertiliser management (the 4Rs)

  • Right source of nutrient for the soil and crop.
  • Right rate based on analysis and yield target.
  • Right time to match crop uptake, e.g. split nitrogen.
  • Right place such as banding phosphorus near the seed.

Over-application wastes money and pollutes water; under-application mines the soil. Manure and compost add nutrients and organic matter but should also be analysed and accounted for in the fertiliser plan.

Safety

Store fertilisers dry, away from fuel; ammonium nitrate is an oxidiser and fire risk. Wear gloves and dust masks when handling lime and fertiliser.

lessons.title: Managing soil health, water and degradation
lessons.html:
Keeping soils productive long term

Conservation agriculture principles

  • Minimum soil disturbance: no-till or reduced tillage protects structure and organic matter.
  • Permanent soil cover: residues and cover crops reduce erosion, conserve moisture and feed soil life.
  • Crop diversity: rotations with legumes and other families break pest cycles and add nitrogen.
  • Integrating livestock to graze cover crops and recycle nutrients, with care not to compact wet soils.

Soil water management

Know your soil's water-holding capacity. Sandy soils hold little water and need frequent light irrigation; clay soils hold more but drain slowly. Use soil moisture probes or tensiometers to schedule irrigation and avoid waterlogging, which drives out oxygen and can cause salinity build-up.

Recognising and repairing degradation

ProblemSignsManagement
CompactionShallow, bent roots, pondingControlled traffic, avoid wet soil, deep ripping where justified, deep-rooted cover crops
AcidificationLow pH, poor legume growthLiming based on analysis
Salinity/sodicityWhite crusts, poor infiltrationDrainage, leaching, gypsum as advised
ErosionRills, gullies, exposed rootsCover, contours, waterways
Organic matter declineCrusting, poor structureResidues, cover crops, manure, less tillage

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 requires land users to protect soil from degradation.

Monitoring soil health

Repeat soil analyses every few years, record yields per field, and use simple field tests: spade tests for structure and roots, infiltration tests, earthworm counts. Track changes over seasons.

Key points

  • Soil health depends on physical, chemical and biological properties together.
  • Sample correctly and base lime and fertiliser on analysis.
  • Apply the 4Rs of nutrient management.
  • Use conservation agriculture to build organic matter and structure.
  • Recognise and correct compaction, acidity, salinity and erosion.
